ourClaim: When you finish, you keep the certificate of completion in your logbook (14 CFR 68.3(b)(1)).
reasoning:
Verified both ground truths. The source text is quoted accurately by the reviewer, and our body does omit "made available upon request" and the name/address/airman-certificate-number contents. But the omission is not a defect, for three reasons.

(1) The omitted clause is not a pilot obligation. 14 CFR 68.3(b) governs items that "must be electronically provided to the individual ... and transmitted to the FAA." The "shall contain the individual's name, address, and airman certificate number" clause is a specification on what the course provider issues; the pilot neither authors nor validates the certificate, so there is no wrong action available to a pilot from its absence.

(2) "Made available upon request" is operationally subsumed by the retention duty our text states correctly. A pilot who does what our body says - keeps the certificate of completion in the logbook - is by construction able to produce it on request. No reading of our sentence leads to non-compliance with the omitted half. (Production of logbook records on request is independently imposed by 61.51(i).)

(3) The refutation checklist's sibling-field test succeeds outright. The adjacent card in the same file, basicmed-cmec-48mo, states: "You keep the completed checklist in your logbook and present it to the FAA on request; it is not mailed to the FAA." The on-request production duty for logbook-retained BasicMed documents is explicitly carried in a sibling record of the same BasicMed requirements set.

Additionally, the body is not a shallow treatment of 68.3(b): it goes on to say "That certificate is not the only thing the course sends," describes the electronic-provision-and-transmission structure of 68.3(b), quotes 68.3(b)(3) verbatim, and connects it to the continuing 61.23(c)(3)(i)(E) care-and-treatment obligation. The envelope's sourceCitation and sourceURL both point to 14 CFR 68.3, which fully supports the claim made, so this is not a provenance mismatch either.

The reviewer concedes in their own "why" that the retained-in-logbook claim is supported. What remains is an exhaustiveness preference about a deliberately summarized field, not a factual error and not something that would mislead a pilot into acting wrongly.

ourClaim: BasicMed applies to private-pilot operations only and does not authorize flying for compensation or hire (14 CFR 61.113(a)).
reasoning:
I tried hard to refute this and could not.

CONFIRMATION 1 - our record says it. `basicmed-overview.body` in /Users/ryan/pilot-medical-guardian-content/v1/basicmed_requirements.json reads verbatim: "BasicMed applies to private-pilot operations only and does not authorize flying for compensation or hire (14 CFR 61.113(a))." I read the whole field. No qualifier appears anywhere else in the body, and no sibling record in the file carries one. The identical unqualified sentence also appears a second time in the `basicmed-operating-limits` record, so the defect is duplicated.

CONFIRMATION 2 - the source says otherwise. The cited paragraph's own first six words are "Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h) of this section". We cite (a) and reproduce its prohibition while dropping (a)'s own governing exception clause. Paragraph (b) then uses the exact phrase permissively: "A private pilot may, for compensation or hire, act as pilot in command of an aircraft in connection with any business or employment if: (1) The flight is only incidental to that business or employment; and (2) The aircraft does not carry passengers or property for compensation or hire." Paragraphs (d) charitable/nonprofit/community event flights under 91.146, (e) search-and-location reimbursement, (f) aircraft salesman demonstration, and (g) glider towing are further exceptions.

REFUTATIONS ATTEMPTED AND FAILED:
- Qualifier elsewhere in the record or a sibling: no. Checked all 7 records in the file; none mentions (b)-(h). The generic "This is a summary of what the FAA requires" tail is not a specific qualifier.
- Provenance-only mismatch: no. The linked document directly contradicts the unqualified claim, so this is substantive, not a citation nicety.
- Rescued by a sibling FAA doc: no. I grepped 61.23 and 68.3/68.7/68.9 for "compensation"/"for hire". Part 68 has zero hits; 61.23's single hit is an unrelated balloon-rating provision. Nothing outside 61.113(a) imposes a compensation bar on BasicMed.
- BasicMed strips the exceptions: no - this is the point that closes it. 61.113(i) conditions the privilege on the pilot "complies with this section and all of the following conditions and limitations" (confirmed verbatim in the corpus). "This section" is the whole of 61.113, so a BasicMed pilot retains exceptions (b) through (h).
- "Private-pilot operations only" already covers it: this is the strongest defense and it half-works. That first clause is accurate. But the second clause does not merely restate it; it misdescribes what private pilot privileges are, adding a blanket prohibition the reg does not contain.

WOULD IT MISLEAD A PILOT: yes, concretely. A BasicMed pilot who flies his own aircraft on a trip incidental to his employment and is reimbursed is expressly permitted by 61.113(b); our text tells him it is not authorized. Likewise a charity/community event flight under 91.146. Pro-rata cost sharing with passengers is universally understood as a compensation question and is read out by the blanket sentence. GA and Class 3 pilots are explicitly in this app's audience, and these are among the most common "can I do this?" questions in general aviation.

SEVERITY - MEDIUM, not HIGH. The error runs in the restrictive direction: it adds a limitation rather than dropping one. A pilot cannot be led into an unsafe or illegal act by it; at worst he declines a flight he was entitled to make, or wrongly concludes he needs a Part 67 medical. The HIGH trigger in the rubric is a dropped restriction that changes the outcome, and this is the inverse. Note this is the documented "permissive-side drift" failure mode already logged in GOTCHAS_CONTENT sections 12 and 17 (we quote restrictive qualifiers verbatim and paraphrase permissive ones away; our claim checks hunt overclaiming and are blind to underselling), which is corroborating rather than dispositive but fits exactly.

Losartan is an ARB (our record's own category field says "ARB (hypertension)"). The ONLY class the worksheet names as unacceptable is "Centrally acting antihypertensive (ex: clonidine)." So row C's unacceptable-medication trigger cannot fire on losartan. Our sentence "Concern is the hypertension, not the drug" is factually correct for this drug: the disposition turns on control, med count, side effects and stability, not on losartan being disallowed.

2. Sibling fields carry every qualifier the reviewer says was dropped. faaStatus is "conditional" (not "acceptable"), isCACI is true, and faaStatusDescription reads: "Hypertension treated with an angiotensin receptor blocker is addressed by the FAA CACI program. Confirm against the current AME Guide CACI - Hypertension worksheet and a qualified AME." That points the pilot at the exact document holding the BP ceiling, the 3-med cap, the 7-day stability requirement and the side-effect criterion. The record never says losartan is auto-issuable.

3. The field is not prose a pilot reads. Grepped the app: treatedConditionNote appears in exactly two places - the property declaration in Reference/FAAMedicationEntry.swift:35 and Reference/Search/ReferenceSearchIndex.swift:100, where it is concatenated into the search-index body alongside faaStatusDescription. There is no display site. A pilot cannot act on a string that is only indexed for typeahead matching.

4. Sibling control. Nine of the eleven ACE/ARB entries set treatedConditionNote to the bare word "Hypertension." The field's semantic job is to NAME the treated condition, not to enumerate DEFER triggers, so "missing" the row-C triggers is not an omission against the field's purpose - no sibling carries them either.

The reviewer generalized row C's trigger to a drug that the FAA's own worksheet places on the allowed list. This is a wording nicety at most, on an unrendered field.
